final_message:
DONE

I pulled the Illinois EPA source water factsheets for all 8 water systems (33 wells, retrieved 2026-11-06), built the Excel file, and wrote the email to your manager with the file attached. **7 of the 33 wells meet all three criteria, and all 7 are in DeWitt County.**

| Rank | System | Well | Depth (ft) | Pumpage* |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Farmer City | WL47648 (Well 9) | 188 | 26,478,500 |
| 2 | Farmer City | WL01130 (Well 11) | 192 | 0 |
| 3 | Farmer City | WL47647 (Well 10) | 181 | 0 |
| 4 | Farmer City | WL47646 (Well 7) | 180 | 21,976,200 |
| 5 | Weldon | WL45047 (Well 3) | 167 | 5,500,000 |
| 6 | Weldon | WL45048 (Well 4) | 163 | 3,503,040 |
| 7 | Waynesville | WL40006 (Well 6) | 162 | 4,319,500 |

*The factsheets don't label pumpage units. The system totals roughly match each town's average daily output × 365, so I treat them as gallons per year and say in both files that this is my inference.

The email recommends the Farmer City wells first. Farmer City has 4 qualifying wells and the largest system of the three towns (about 257,000 gallons/day), and Well 9 has the most recorded pumpage of any well that passed. Weldon is the backup. Waynesville is last: it is a very small system, and a leaking fuel-tank cleanup site sits 50 ft from the well.

The other five systems have no well that passes:
- **Springerton, Enfield and Crossville:** every listed well is abandoned.
- **Bartlett:** every well is sealed, abandoned, disconnected or emergency-only.
- **Norris City:** both active wells are too shallow (97 and 124 ft).

Things to resolve before relying on these wells:
- **Farmer City Well 7:** the well table lists it as active, but the factsheet's own text calls it inactive. It still passes the screen as written, so I kept it but ranked it 4th and flagged it.
- **Farmer City Wells 10 and 11:** both show 0 pumpage, even though the factsheet text names them as supply wells. Current output should be confirmed with the city.
- **Access:** these are town water-supply wells, so using them would mean a water purchase agreement with the town or drilling our own well in the same aquifer. A new well that can pump 100,000 gallons/day or more requires notifying the county Soil and Water Conservation District before construction.
- **Water demand:** the facility size wasn't given, so I didn't compare demand to well output. The email gives a scale example using DOE figures: a plant making 1,000 kg of hydrogen per day would consume about 2,400–8,000 gallons of water per day.

The screening columns are Excel formulas with no stored results, because no spreadsheet program was available here to calculate them. Excel calculates them on open, but some preview tools may show those columns blank. I didn't use the Status code (A/I) as a criterion, since the assignment defines "active" by the well description. That is why Bartlett Wells 4 and 6 are excluded even though they are coded active: they are marked "emergency".

The email cites the IEPA factsheet site, DOE's water-use-in-hydrogen-production record, and a CMAP (Chicago regional planning agency) summary of the high-capacity well rules, each with its retrieval date. The state statute's text was blocked when I tried to retrieve it, so the email says those rules come from the CMAP summary. Names and the recipient are placeholders to fill in.

Files are in `outputs/`:
- `IL_SWAP_Well_Screening_Green_H2.xlsx`: "All Wells" tab (all 33 wells, a filter on each criterion, and a "MEETS ALL CRITERIA?" column) and "Potential Wells" tab (the 7 ranked wells with notes)
- `Email_to_Manager_Well_Recommendation.docx`: the email
- `Email_to_Manager_Well_Recommendation.eml`: the same email as an unsent draft with the Excel file attached
